title: Using Artificial Intelligence Algorithms to Predict Self-Reported Problem Gambling Among Online Casino Gamblers from Different Countries Using Account-Based Player Data
authors: Hopfgartner, N.; Auer, M.; Helic, D.; Griffiths, M. D.
venue: International Journal of Mental Health and Addiction
tldr: Tests five ML models to predict self-reported problem gambling across 1,743 British, Canadian, and Spanish online casino gamblers, finding behavioral variables more predictive than monetary ones.
problem_and_motivation: Online gambling operators need predictive models for early detection of problem gambling, but existing research lacks cross-country validation and clarity on whether behavioral or monetary variables are most predictive.
approach: Used a secondary dataset of 1,743 online casino gamblers from Britain, Canada, and Spain (39% female, mean age 42.4).
Employed hierarchical logistic regression to examine demographic, behavioral, and monetary intensity associations.
Tested five machine learning models to predict self-reported problem gambling (PGSI >=8).
Compared model performance with and without country-specific training data.
Analyzed behavioral variables including self-exclusions, in-session deposits, and account depletion.
findings: num: 27.4% of participants scored 8+ on the PGSI (problem gambling threshold).
Behavioral variables (self-exclusions, frequent deposits, account depletion) were paramount over monetary intensity variables.
Machine learning models effectively predicted problem gambling across countries without country-specific training data.
Incorporating country-specific data improved overall model performance.
Specific behavioral patterns are universal, with nuanced cross-country differences.

topics.name: Classification Approaches for Financial Behavioral Profiles

topics.name: Predictive Modeling in Personal Finance Systems

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: This paper demonstrates that behavioral variables (self-exclusions, deposit patterns, account depletion) are more predictive of problem gambling than monetary intensity variables. It shows that ML models can generalize across countries without country-specific training, though incorporating such data improves performance. The cross-country design advances understanding of universal versus context-specific behavioral risk markers.
directly_justifies: Behavioral variables predict problem gambling better than monetary intensity measures.
ML models predict problem gambling across countries without country-specific training data.
Country-specific training data improves cross-national model performance.
limits: Dataset from a single operator may not represent the broader online casino population.
Self-reported PGSI as ground truth has known limitations.
Results may not generalize to other gambling modalities (sports betting, poker).
topic_relevance.topic_mapping_rationale: Systematic scan across all 14 topic domains was performed. Domain 5 (Profiles and Classification) was flagged as high relevance because ML classification of behavioral risk profiles is the core methodology. Domain 6 (Predictive Modeling) was flagged as high for the same reason. All other domains (1-4, 7-14) were rejected as the paper addresses gambling risk detection, not personal finance systems.

limitations: Secondary dataset from a single operator may introduce selection bias.
PGSI self-report as ground truth may not capture all forms of gambling harm.
Limited to online casino gamblers; other modalities excluded.
remember_this: Behavioral variables predict problem gambling better than monetary variables.
ML models generalize across countries without country-specific training.
27.4% of online casino gamblers scored PGSI 8+ (problem gambling).
Cross-country approach reveals both universal and context-specific risk patterns.
